summary: Mining study deriving a taxonomy of runtime faults in MCP servers: from 1,774 public repos filtered to 473 maintained ones, then 200 fault-richest repos, keyword filtering and manual review yield 833 confirmed fault threads, coded into 11 categories, 27 subcategories, 73 leaf types. A survey of 55 MCP practitioners (≈4.6% response) checks recognition, severity and diagnostic effort.

claims.claim: Taxonomy of 11 categories / 27 subcategories / 73 leaf types from 833 fault threads.
claims.evidence: §4.6 coding in five rounds by two authors, final-round Cohen's kappa 0.938 with 52 disagreements; saturation asserted.

claims.claim: Tool (23.0%), Data & Schema (17.6%) and State & Configuration (17.1%) dominate, i.e., failures concentrate in capability execution and schema enforcement rather than transport.
claims.evidence: §6 counts 192/147/143 of 833. Authors note these are descriptive of a criterion-selected sample (top-200 fault-rich repos), not prevalence estimates (§7 Conclusion validity).

claims.claim: Respondents experienced on average 20 of the 27 subcategories; no category unobserved.
claims.evidence: Inconsistent with body: §5.12 reports an average confirmation rate of 44% per subcategory (≈12 of 27), with least-reported categories at 25%. Survey also assessed a provisional 45-item taxonomy, not the final 27 subcategories (§4.6).

claims.claim: Some faults return well-formed JSON-RPC success while violating semantics (gray failures), so oracles must check behavior, not just errors.

patterns.note: MCP integration layer has recurring server-side runtime faults (schema, state, initialization, result propagation).
Recommends conformance tests derived from leaf categories and behavioral oracles; not evaluated.
Taxonomy proposed as triage labels; silent-success failures argue for content-level monitoring.

methodology.sample: 473 repos mined (≤200 recent issues/PRs each), 200 selected for manual analysis, 833 confirmed threads; survey n=55 from ~1,200 invited.
methodology.variance: Inter-rater kappa reported; survey descriptive percentages only.
methodology.languages: Not broken down by implementation language in the text reviewed; GitHub-only, English-only.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint (17 pages); no venue listed.
standards.artifacts: Replication package on figshare with mined datasets, coding records, scripts.

biases.detail: Only closed, bug-labelled, English, publicly discussed threads; private/enterprise faults absent (acknowledged §7).
4.6% response rate, purposive sampling; respondents rated a provisional 45-item version.
Abstract's 'average of 20 of 27 subcategories' conflicts with §5.12's 44% average confirmation rate.
Survey 'no new category emerged' is weak evidence of completeness given low response rate.

coi.affiliations: JADS / Tilburg University, University of Sannio, University of Luxembourg, Gran Sasso Science Institute.
coi.funding: Safeguard project (grant 20506020) and funding from Deloitte; COI statement declares none.
coi.detail: Industry funding (Deloitte) but no product evaluated.

verdict_reason: Careful, replicable qualitative taxonomy with high inter-rater agreement and released data; caveats are the unexplained abstract/body mismatch on survey results, the survey validating a provisional taxonomy, and frequency counts from a criterion-selected sample.
applicability: If the Java team exposes ingestion or content-delivery capabilities as MCP servers for mixed agent hosts, the taxonomy is a ready checklist for conformance tests: validate inputs against declared inputSchema, gate requests on initialization, preserve JSON-RPC ids, keep logs off stdout for stdio transport, and assert response content (silent-success faults). It is server-side only — it says nothing about host/client/orchestration faults or cross-repo contracts — and gives no evidence specific to Java SDKs.
